segments.say: We built a specialist on day one, and it worked. So start today with the honest question: what can that specialist not do? I am asking it directly, about our own project. If I wanted six of these building different parts of Control Tower at the same time, where does the idea break? And the answer is precise. A sub-agent exists to serve the session that called it. You cannot talk to it. It cannot talk to anything except whoever started it. And it lives exactly as long as its task, then its context is gone. Which is fine for send someone to read this and report back. It is useless for six people building one product, because the moment two of them need to agree on something, there is no channel for them to agree on. And be clear that this is not a flaw in sub-agents. It is a design choice, and it is the right one for what they are for. A sub-agent is cheap precisely because it is disposable: it goes away, and all you keep is the answer. Everything expensive about a team comes from the opposite decision — keeping them alive, and letting them talk. And the answer on screen is more specific than three properties. Six headings, and not one of them is about how clever the agent is. They cannot talk to each other. They share one working tree. Their boundaries are promises, not walls. They cannot ask anyone anything mid-run. Only one of them can run the app. And you see nothing until they finish, and only a compressed report then. The third is the one people get wrong: the simulator agent's brief says source sim and nothing outside it, but its tools are read, write, edit and bash over the whole filesystem. The brief steers. It does not enforce. And the fifth would have bitten us tonight: everything here serves on port eight zero eight zero, so if the API agent and the tester both start the server to check their own work, the second one fails to bind. Verification is a shared resource, and cleverness does not fix it. It is worth holding those three properties in your head, because they are the whole distinction and everything else follows from them. It serves one caller. It has one channel. It dies with its task. Any time you are unsure which of the two things you want, ask which of those three you would have to break.

So here is the thing that does work, and the differences are worth naming one at a time. Each teammate gets its own full context window — not a slice of yours, its own. They are not returned to the caller and folded back in; they persist while the work does. They can message each other directly, without routing everything through you. They share one task list, so there is a single place that says who is doing what. And you can talk to any of them, not just the one in charge. And then the part I asked for on purpose: when is a sub-agent still the better choice? Because the answer is often. If the job is go and find something out and come back, a team is expensive theatre. Reach for a team when the work genuinely has to be divided and the pieces have to agree. There is a cost to every one of those differences, and you should hear it now rather than discover it. Six independent context windows means six times the reading. Messages between teammates are themselves tokens. And a shared task list only helps if the work genuinely divides — if two agents keep needing the same file, you have not built a team, you have built a queue with extra steps. The honest test is this: could you hand these pieces to six different people who only spoke to each other twice a day? If yes, a team will work. If they would be in each other's way constantly, you want one agent and a clear order of work.

And there is a scheduling point buried in that test which is easy to skip past. Work that divides cleanly is not a property of the work. It is a property of how well the interfaces between the pieces are written down. Two agents on the same file is a queue. Two agents on either side of a contract you wrote out in full is a team. Which means the effort you put into the plan is not preparation for the team - it is what determines whether a team is possible at all. And the answer on screen is honest about what a team does not fix. Teams do not repeal the physical constraints. It is still one repo, so six teammates in one checkout still race on package dot json and the tests directory. The port is still eight zero eight zero and only one process binds it. The simulator boundary is still a promise rather than a wall. Teams fix the coordination gaps; the shared-resource gaps you still have to design around yourself. Then it lists when a sub-agent is still the better choice, and it is a longer list than the marketing suggests. When the task is a leaf: fully specified, no negotiation, report as the deliverable. When what you want is context hygiene rather than parallelism — you want the conclusion, not the forty file reads. When the work is read-only fan-out. And when you want one mind holding the integration, because a team distributes understanding and sometimes you want it concentrated. Its rule of thumb for this repo is the sentence to keep: the interlocking middle of the plan is team-shaped, and the edges stay sub-agent-shaped. Now the practical bit, and notice how it answers. I asked what exactly goes in settings for this to work, and what the valid values are — and to check the installed version rather than telling me what it remembers. So it goes and looks at the program on this machine. An environment variable that marks the feature experimental, and a teammate mode with a small set of accepted values. One of those values is new since most of what is written about this online, which is exactly why I asked it to check. Watch the trace rather than the conclusion. It runs the installed binary to get the version, then greps the bundle: three patterns, one directory, two shell commands — then two more patterns, and two more after that. It confirms the mode values, then says it still needs the exact enablement gate and goes looking again. Nearly two minutes and four thousand tokens, to establish two strings. That is what checking costs, and it is cheaper than being confidently wrong in front of six agents. If you take one habit from today, take that one: when the answer is a flag name, make it read the binary, not its memory. And one honest caveat before we go further. This is still marked experimental. It may be more settled by the time you watch this — and if the flag has gone entirely, that is good news, not a broken lecture. And one more thing about how it answered, because it is the pattern I keep pointing at. It did not tell me the flag from memory and it did not tell me confidently and wrongly. It went and read the thing installed on this machine. Every week these tools change. The skill that lasts is not knowing the current flag names — it is having the habit of making the agent check. And there is a broader version of that habit worth stating plainly, because it applies to everything in this week. When the answer is a fact about the world, ask for the source. When the answer is a fact about the software on this machine, make it read the software on this machine. The failure mode these tools have is not being wrong. It is being wrong in the exact register of being right.
